mainTopic: The testimonies of יוסי בן יועזר (locusts, slaughterhouse liquids, touching a מת), and the source for forbidding a נכרי's cooked food.
overview: The amud opens by finishing the dispute about a kosher locust. Everyone agrees a long-headed locust is forbidden. The argument is only about whether wings that barely cover most of the body are enough. Next comes יוסי בן יועזר's testimony that the Temple slaughterhouse liquids are pure. רב and שמואל argue over what 'pure' means, based on how much of טומאת משקין is from the Torah. The גמרא then asks why יוסי בן יועזר was called 'the Permitter' for ruling that touching a מת makes one impure. A first explanation about chains of touching is rejected by רבא. רבא says that, according to רב נחמן, יוסי בן יועזר publicly ruled that a ספק טומאה in a רשות הרבים is טהור. Finally the גמרא looks for the source that a נכרי's cooked food (שלקות) is forbidden. It learns it from משה's request to buy food and water from סיחון, and keeps refining what kind of change counts. The amud ends with a challenge to the 'change by fire' answer, which continues on the next amud.

steps.title: Where exactly the locust dispute lies
steps.stepSummary: Everyone agrees a long-headed locust (a סוסביל) is forbidden. The dispute is only about a locust whose wings barely cover most of its body.
steps.simpleTranslation: It is a סוסביל. So about a long-headed locust, everyone agrees it is forbidden. The argument is about one whose wings cover most of its body, but only barely.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא narrows the argument between יוסי בן יועזר and the רבנן about the locust. It takes the long-headed case out of the dispute and puts the dispute on the wing-coverage case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Earlier it looked as if the רבנן and יוסי בן יועזר argued about a long-headed locust. The גמרא now says no one permits that one. The real case is a locust whose wings cover most of its body only by a small margin.

keyTerms.meaning: Name of a type of locust that is forbidden
Its wings cover most of its body, one of the signs of a kosher locust

phrases.english: it is a susbil,
phrases.notes: A long-headed locust is called a סוסביל.

phrases.english: so with regard to a long-headed one,
everyone agrees that it is forbidden;
and here, about one whose wings cover most of it
only barely, is where they disagree:

steps.triggerLanguage: כּוּלֵּי עָלְמָא לָא פְּלִיגִי דְּאָסוּר, וְהָכָא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Ends the earlier discussion of the locust by redefining the case under dispute.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the case (אוקימתא): the dispute is moved from a long-headed locust to a locust with barely-covering wings.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We might have thought the dispute was about a long-headed locust.
steps.terutzMaskana: A long-headed locust is forbidden by all. The dispute is only about wings that barely cover most of the body.

steps.title: Bare majority versus noticeable majority
steps.stepSummary: One side holds that any majority, even a tiny one, is enough. The other side requires a majority you can clearly see.
steps.simpleTranslation: One Sage holds that any majority at all is enough. The other Sage holds that we need a majority that is clearly noticeable.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא explains the reasoning behind the two sides of the locust dispute.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Both sides agree the wings must cover most of the body. They argue over what counts as 'most'. יוסי בן יועזר accepts a bare majority, so he permits this locust. The רבנן need a visible majority, so they forbid it.

keyTerms.meaning: Any majority at all, even a tiny one

steps.whatToRemember: The locust dispute comes down to the definition of 'majority' (רוב). Is a bare majority enough, or must the majority be clearly noticeable?

phrases.aramaic: מָר סָבַר רוּבָּא כֹּל דְּהוּ בָּעֵינַן,
phrases.english: one Sage holds we require any majority at all,
phrases.notes: This is יוסי בן יועזר, who permitted the locust.

phrases.english: and one Sage holds we require a noticeable majority.
phrases.notes: This is the רבנן, who forbid it.

steps.triggerLanguage: מָר סָבַר רוּבָּא כֹּל דְּהוּ בָּעֵינַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Gives the reasoning for the dispute that step 1 located.
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The two sides argue only about whether a minimal majority of wing coverage is enough or a noticeable majority is needed.

steps.title: Testimony: the Temple slaughterhouse liquids are pure
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes the next testimony of יוסי בן יועזר: the liquids in the slaughterhouse of the בית המקדש are pure.
steps.simpleTranslation: And he testified about the liquids of the slaughterhouse that they are pure.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא moves to a new topic. It quotes the next part of the testimony so it can examine it in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This is the second testimony of יוסי בן יועזר. It deals with the water and blood in the Temple's slaughter area. The word 'דכן' (pure) is left unclear, and the next step asks about it.

keyTerms.meaning: The liquids (water and blood) of the slaughterhouse in the בית המקדש

phrases.english: And about the liquids of the slaughterhouse, that they are pure.
phrases.notes: This quotes the testimony of יוסי בן יועזר that was brought earlier in the sugya.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, the next item in the same set of testimonies.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The liquids of the Temple slaughterhouse are pure.

steps.title: What does 'pure' mean here?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks what kind of purity יוסי בן יועזר meant.
steps.simpleTranslation: What does 'pure' mean?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks a clarifying question about the word דכן. It is setting up the argument between רב and שמואל.
steps.deeperAnalysis: 'Pure' could mean fully pure, so the liquid can never become impure. It could also mean partly pure, so the liquid can become impure itself but cannot pass impurity on to other things. The question opens both options.

phrases.english: What does 'pure' mean?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the meaning of the key word in the testimony just quoted.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: How far the purity of the slaughterhouse liquids goes.

steps.title: רב: fully pure; שמואל: pure only toward others
steps.stepSummary: רב says the liquids are completely pure. שמואל says they cannot make other things impure, but they can become impure themselves.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said: truly pure. שמואל said: pure in that they do not make other things impure, but they themselves can become impure.
steps.whatsHappening: Two אמוראים answer the question, and each gives a different meaning for 'pure'.
steps.deeperAnalysis: For רב, impurity cannot take hold of these liquids at all. For שמואל, the liquid can become impure, but it cannot pass that impurity on to food or vessels.

keyTerms.meaning: Their own impurity, meaning they themselves become impure

steps.confusionAlert: Do not mix up 'becoming impure' with 'making others impure'. שמואל splits these two. The liquid itself can become impure, but it cannot pass impurity along.

phrases.english: Rav said: actually pure,
and Shmuel said: pure in that they do not make others impure,
but they themselves can become impure.

steps.triggerLanguage: רַב אָמַר: דְּכַן מַמָּשׁ, וּשְׁמוּאֵל אָמַר
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 4 with two opinions.
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: רב: completely pure. שמואל: they do not pass impurity to others but can become impure themselves.

steps.title: Why רב says the liquids are fully pure
steps.stepSummary: רב holds that all impurity of liquids comes only from the רבנן. The רבנן never made their decree for the Temple slaughterhouse liquids.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב said 'truly pure' because he holds that the impurity of liquids is only rabbinic. When the Rabbis decreed impurity, it was on ordinary liquids. They did not decree it on the liquids of the slaughterhouse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats רב's words in order to explain the reason behind them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the Torah gives liquids no impurity at all, then everything depends on the Rabbis' decree. Since that decree never covered the Temple slaughterhouse, those liquids have no impurity of any kind.

keyTerms.meaning: From the Rabbis, not from the Torah

phrases.english: Rav said: 'actually pure,'
because he holds: the impurity of liquids is rabbinic,

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי גְּזוּר רַבָּנַן טוּמְאָה בְּמַשְׁקִין דְּעָלְמָא,
phrases.english: and when the Rabbis decreed impurity, it was on ordinary liquids,

phrases.aramaic: אֲבָל בְּמַשְׁקֵה בֵּי מַטְבְּחַיָּא לָא גְּזַרוּ רַבָּנַן.
phrases.english: but on the liquids of the slaughterhouse the Rabbis did not decree.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the reasoning behind רב's opinion from step 5.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: All impurity of liquids is rabbinic, and the decree was never made for the slaughterhouse liquids, so they are fully pure.

steps.title: Why שמואל says they still become impure themselves
steps.stepSummary: שמואל holds that a liquid becoming impure is from the Torah, while its passing impurity to others is only rabbinic. The rabbinic part was never decreed for the slaughterhouse.
steps.simpleTranslation: שמואל said they are pure in that they do not make others impure, but they themselves can become impure. He holds that the impurity of liquids themselves is from the Torah, and their making others impure is from the Rabbis. When the Rabbis decreed, it was on ordinary liquids. On the slaughterhouse liquids they did not decree.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא repeats שמואל's words in order to explain his reasoning.
steps.deeperAnalysis: שמואל splits the impurity of liquids into two levels. The Torah level (becoming impure) cannot be removed by the Rabbis, so it applies even in the Temple. The rabbinic level (passing impurity on) was never decreed for the slaughterhouse.
steps.whatToRemember: רב: all impurity of liquids is rabbinic, so the slaughterhouse liquids are completely pure. שמואל: a liquid becoming impure is from the Torah, while passing impurity to others is rabbinic. So the slaughterhouse liquids only lose the rabbinic part.
steps.whyThisMatters: The dispute shows a key question in the laws of purity: is the impurity of liquids from the Torah or from the Rabbis? That question decides how far a rabbinic exemption can reach.

phrases.english: And Shmuel said: pure in that they do not make others impure,
but they themselves can become impure,
because he holds: the impurity of liquids themselves is from the Torah,
but their making others impure is rabbinic,
and when the Rabbis decreed, it was on ordinary liquids;
on the liquids of the slaughterhouse they did not decree.

steps.triggerLanguage: קָסָבַר: טוּמְאַת מַשְׁקִין דְּאוֹרָיְיתָא לְטַמֵּא אֲחֵרִים דְּרַבָּנַן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains שמואל's opinion, parallel to the explanation of רב in step 6.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: Liquids becoming impure is from the Torah and stays in force. Passing impurity to others is rabbinic and was not decreed for the slaughterhouse liquids.

steps.title: Third testimony: touching a dead body makes one impure
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא quotes יוסי בן יועזר's third testimony: one who touches a מת is טמא. Because of this, people called him 'יוסף שריא', the Permitter.
steps.simpleTranslation: And about one who touches a dead body, he testified that the person is impure. And people called him 'Yosef the Permitter.'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא quotes the next testimony of יוסי בן יועזר and the strange nickname people gave him for it. This sets up the questions that follow.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The testimony sounds strict, since it says someone is impure. Yet the nickname says he was lenient. This mismatch is exactly what the גמרא will question next.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who permits; the lenient one

phrases.english: And regarding one who touches a dead body: he is impure,
phrases.notes: This is the third of יוסי בן יועזר's testimonies. The גמרא already went through the first two.

phrases.english: and they called him 'Yosef the Permitter.'

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves on from the testimony about liquids in the slaughterhouse to the next testimony in the same list.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: One who touches a מת is טמא, and יוסי בן יועזר was nicknamed 'the Permitter' for this testimony.

steps.title: Why call him lenient, and isn't this already in the Torah?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא makes two attacks. First, a strict ruling should earn the name 'Yosef the Forbidder'. Second, the Torah already says plainly that touching a מת makes one טמא, so why would anyone need to testify about it?
steps.simpleTranslation: They should have called him 'Yosef the Forbidder'! And furthermore, this is from the Torah, as it is written: 'And whoever in the open field touches one slain by the sword, or a dead body...'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the testimony from two directions. The nickname doesn't fit, and the ruling seems to add nothing new.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Attack one is about the nickname: calling someone impure is strict, not lenient. Attack two is about the testimony itself: a פסוק already says this, so a testimony seems pointless. Any answer must explain both.

keyTerms.meaning: The one who forbids; the strict one
It should have been; it needed to say
From the Torah (as opposed to from the רבנן)

phrases.english: They should have called him 'Yosef the Forbidder'!
And furthermore, it is from the Torah,
as it is written:
'And whoever touches, in the open field,
one slain by the sword, or a dead body, etc.'!
phrases.notes: במדבר 19:16

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks both the nickname and the need for the testimony quoted in step 8.
steps.kashyaTarget: The nickname 'יוסף שריא' and the need for a testimony at all
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A strict ruling cannot earn a lenient nickname, and a law written openly in the Torah needs no testimony.

steps.title: He restored the Torah law against a rabbinic decree
steps.stepSummary: Under the Torah, only one who touches the מת itself is טמא. Someone who touches that person stays טהור. The רבנן decreed that this second person is also טמא. יוסי בן יועזר testified that the הלכה goes back to the Torah level, which makes him lenient.
steps.simpleTranslation: By Torah law, one who touches a dead body is impure, but one who touches someone who touched it is pure. The Rabbis came and decreed impurity even on one who touches someone who touched. Then he came and set the law back on the Torah level.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers both questions at once. The testimony was really about the second-level person, and on that point it was a leniency.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The point of the testimony was not 'the toucher is impure'. It was 'only the toucher is impure, not the one who touches him'. That answers the nickname question, since he cancelled a strict גזירה. It also answers the 'it's already in the Torah' question, since the new point was that the rabbinic extension was removed.

keyTerms.meaning: He set it up; he established it

phrases.english: By Torah law, one who touches [the dead body] is impure,
one who touches someone who touched is pure,
and they came and decreed
phrases.notes: 'They' means the רבנן.

phrases.english: even on one who touches someone who touched,
and he came and set it back on the Torah law.
phrases.notes: 'He' is יוסי בן יועזר.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers both parts of the question in step 9.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterprets the testimony as cancelling a rabbinic decree
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The testimony was a strict statement that touching a מת makes one impure.
steps.terutzMaskana: The testimony limited טומאה to the Torah level, so the second-level toucher is טהור. That is a leniency.

steps.title: A verse shows the second toucher is impure by Torah law too
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the answer. A פסוק says 'whatever the impure person touches shall be impure'. So touching someone who touched a מת also seems to bring טומאה from the Torah, not just from the רבנן.
steps.simpleTranslation: One who touches someone who touched is also impure by Torah law, as it is written: 'And whatever the impure person touches shall be impure'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the previous answer. It argues that the second-level toucher is impure from the Torah itself.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 10 said that under the Torah the second toucher is טהור. This פסוק seems to say the opposite. If so, there was no rabbinic decree for יוסי בן יועזר to cancel.

phrases.english: One who touches someone who touched, too,
is impure by Torah law,
as it is written:
'And whatever the impure person touches shall be impure'!
phrases.notes: במדבר 19:22

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the claim in step 10 that the second toucher is pure under the Torah.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that under the Torah, one who touches someone who touched a מת is טהור
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: במדבר 19:22 makes the second-level toucher impure from the Torah, which would leave no rabbinic decree to cancel.

steps.title: רב נחמן: the Torah law depends on whether the contact is still connected
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן explains the Torah law. If the middle person is still touching the מת while someone touches him (חיבורין), that person gets seven-day טומאה. If not, the טומאה lasts only until evening. The רבנן decreed seven-day טומאה even without that connection. יוסי בן יועזר brought the law back to the Torah level.
steps.simpleTranslation: The Rabbis said this before רבא in the name of מר זוטרא son of רב נחמן, who said in the name of רב נחמן: By Torah law, one who touches someone who touched a dead body gets seven-day impurity if the contact is still connected, and impurity until evening if it is not. The Rabbis came and decreed seven-day impurity even without connection. Then he came and set the law back on the Torah level.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a sharper answer that fits the פסוק. The second toucher is impure by Torah law, but the length of the impurity depends on the connection.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The פסוק is accepted: the second toucher is impure from the Torah. The rabbinic decree was about how long, not whether. The רבנן made it seven days even without connection. יוסי בן יועזר cancelled that extension, so he was still a lenient 'שריא'.

keyTerms.meaning: Connection: the middle person is still touching the מת at the same time

steps.whatToRemember: In this explanation, someone who touches a person who touched a מת is impure for seven days under the Torah only if that person is still touching the מת. Otherwise it lasts only until evening. On this view, יוסי בן יועזר cancelled the רבנן's seven-day extension, which earned him the name 'the Permitter'. רבא rejects this explanation in step 15.
steps.confusionAlert: Don't mix up step 10 and step 12. In step 10 the second toucher was fully טהור under the Torah. In this answer he is טמא under the Torah, and the only question is seven days versus one day. This answer is itself rejected by רבא in step 15.

phrases.english: The Rabbis said it before Rava,

phrases.aramaic: מִשְּׁמֵיהּ דְּמָר זוּטְרָא בְּרֵיהּ דְּרַב נַחְמָן,
phrases.english: in the name of Mar Zutra son of Rav Nachman,
who said in the name of Rav Nachman:
By Torah law, one who touches someone who touched:
while connected, seven-day impurity,
phrases.notes: 'Connected' means the middle person is still touching the dead body at that moment.

phrases.english: while not connected, impurity until evening,
and they came and decreed
even when not connected, seven-day impurity,
and he came and set it back on the Torah law.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge in step 11 by accepting the פסוק and moving the rabbinic decree from 'whether impure' to 'how long impure'.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Splits the case by connection to the מת
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Under the Torah the second toucher is fully טהור, and the decree made him טמא.
steps.terutzMaskana: Under the Torah the second toucher is impure for seven days if connected and until evening if not. The decree extended seven days to the unconnected case, and יוסי בן יועזר cancelled it.
steps.whyThisMatters: This sets out the Torah-level rule of חיבורין for corpse impurity: how long the טומאה lasts depends on whether the contact happens while still connected to the מת.

steps.title: What is the Torah source? Three verses that seem to clash
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks for the Torah source of the חיבורין rule. It quotes three פסוקים: two point to seven-day טומאה for the second person, and one says only until evening.
steps.simpleTranslation: What is the Torah law based on? It is written: 'One who touches a dead person shall be impure seven days.' It is also written: 'Whatever the impure person touches shall be impure.' And it is also written: 'The person who touches shall be impure until evening.' How do these fit together?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks where the Torah law from רב נחמן's explanation in step 12 comes from. It lines up three פסוקים that seem to contradict each other and asks how they fit. This sets up the answer in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The first two פסוקים read together suggest that the person who touches someone טמא מת is also טמא for seven days. The third פסוק says such a person is טמא only until evening. 'הא כיצד' asks how both can be true.

keyTerms.meaning: As it is written (introduces a פסוק)
Seven days, the full length of טומאת מת
Until evening, a light one-day טומאה
How so? How do these fit together?

phrases.english: What is the Torah law based on?
phrases.notes: He means the Torah law רב נחמן described in step 12.

phrases.english: As it is written: "One who touches a dead body
of any human being
shall be impure seven days,"
phrases.notes: במדבר 19:11

phrases.aramaic: וּכְתִיב: ״וְכֹל אֲשֶׁר יִגַּע בּוֹ הַטָּמֵא יִטְמָא״,
phrases.english: and it is written: "And whatever the impure person touches shall be impure,"
phrases.notes: במדבר 19:22. Together with the first פסוק, this suggests the second person also gets seven days.

phrases.english: and it is written: "And the person who touches
shall be impure until evening."
phrases.notes: Same פסוק, במדבר 19:22, second half.

phrases.english: How can this be?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the Torah source of רב נחמן's distinction in step 12
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Which פסוקים teach the Torah-level split between seven-day and until-evening טומאה for one who touches a טמא מת, and how do they fit together?

steps.title: The verses fit: connected versus not connected
steps.stepSummary: The seven-day פסוקים are about someone touching the טמא מת while that person is still touching the מת. The until-evening פסוק is about when there is no such connection.
steps.simpleTranslation: Here it is talking about when they are connected. There it is talking about when they are not connected.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא settles the clash between the פסוקים. Each פסוק is about a different case.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If the middle person is still touching the מת (חיבורין), whoever touches him becomes טמא for seven days. If the middle person has let go, whoever touches him is טמא only until evening. This gives a Torah basis to רב נחמן's explanation in step 12.

keyTerms.meaning: Here... there; the standard way to split two sources into two cases
Connection: the middle person is still touching the מת at that moment

phrases.english: Here, it is when they are connected;
phrases.notes: 'Here' is the two seven-day פסוקים.

phrases.english: there, it is when they are not connected.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of step 13 by assigning each פסוק to a different case
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The seven-day פסוקים are about חיבורין; the until-evening פסוק is about no חיבורין.
steps.whatToRemember: By Torah law, touching a טמא מת gives seven days only with חיבורין; otherwise it lasts until evening. This was the basis for calling יוסי בן יועזר lenient. The next step will reject this explanation.

steps.title: רבא: Don't pin false statements on רב נחמן
steps.stepSummary: רבא rejects the whole חיבורין explanation. He says it was never said by רב נחמן.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבא said to them: Didn't I tell you not to hang empty jugs on רב נחמן?
steps.whatsHappening: רבא rejects the explanation from steps 12–14. He says it was wrongly credited to רב נחמן.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבא does not argue with the logic of the פסוקים. He attacks the attribution and says רב נחמן never said this. That leaves the question 'why was he called the Permitter?' open again, and רבא will give the real version next.

keyTerms.meaning: Empty jugs: a picture for empty, made-up statements

steps.confusionAlert: The text does not say whether רבא rejects the חיבורין rule itself as Torah law. What he clearly rejects is the claim that it is the explanation רב נחמן gave for why יוסי בן יועזר was called the Permitter.

phrases.english: רבא said to them:
Didn't I tell you
not to hang empty jugs
phrases.notes: It's a saying: don't pin made-up statements on someone.

phrases.english: on רב נחמן?

steps.triggerLanguage: לָאו אָמֵינָא לְכוּ לָא תִּתְלוֹ בֵּיהּ בּוּקֵי סְרִיקֵי בְּרַב נַחְמָן
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the attribution of the explanation built in steps 12–14
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole חיבורין explanation of why יוסי בן יועזר was called the Permitter
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: It was falsely credited to רב נחמן; he never said it.

steps.title: What רב נחמן really said: a doubt in a public area is permitted
steps.stepSummary: רבא gives רב נחמן's true explanation: יוסי בן יועזר ruled that a ספק טומאה in a רשות הרבים is טהור.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what רב נחמן said: He permitted for them a case of doubtful טומאה in a public area.
steps.whatsHappening: רבא gives the correct version of רב נחמן's words. This is a new explanation of why יוסי בן יועזר was called the Permitter.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The leniency is now about doubt, not about chains of touching. If a person is unsure whether he touched טומאה in a רשות הרבים, יוסי בן יועזר ruled that he is טהור. That ruling earned him the name 'the Permitter'.

keyTerms.meaning: A doubt whether someone became טמא
Public domain, a place where many people pass

phrases.english: This is what רב נחמן said:
a case of doubtful טומאה in a public area
he permitted for them.
phrases.notes: 'He' is יוסי בן יועזר. This ruling is why he was called the Permitter.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Replaces the rejected explanation with רב נחמן's true words
steps.mimraCoreRuling: יוסי בן יועזר ruled that a ספק טומאה in a רשות הרבים is טהור.
steps.whyThisMatters: This is the well-known rule that a ספק טומאה in a public area is treated as טהור.

steps.title: But that rule is already learned from סוטה
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא objects that the rule about doubts in a public area is already known from סוטה. So what did יוסי בן יועזר add?
steps.simpleTranslation: But isn't this a law we learn from סוטה? Just as a סוטה is about a private area, so too טומאה is about a private area.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן's true explanation from step 16. It points out that this rule is already learned from the laws of סוטה.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A סוטה is only forbidden because of doubt when the suspected act happened in a private area. טומאה is compared to סוטה, so a ספק טומאה makes someone טמא only in a רשות היחיד. That means a doubt in a public area is already טהור, and it seems יוסי בן יועזר had nothing new to permit. This is the same kind of attack as in step 9.

keyTerms.meaning: A woman whose husband suspects her of being unfaithful

phrases.english: But isn't it an established law
that we learn from סוטה:
just as סוטה is about a private area,
so too doubtful טומאה is only in a private area!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the new explanation in step 16
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's claim that יוסי בן יועזר permitted ספק טומאה in a רשות הרבים
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The comparison to סוטה already teaches that a doubt is only טמא in a private area. So a doubt in a public area is already טהור, and there was nothing left for יוסי בן יועזר to permit.

steps.title: It was the הלכה, but nobody ruled that way in public
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן explains that the leniency was always the הלכה but was not taught publicly. יוסי בן יועזר's new contribution was to make it an official ruling.
steps.simpleTranslation: But רבי יוחנן said: it is the הלכה, yet we do not issue a ruling that way. So יוסי בן יועזר came and made it an official ruling.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the question from step 17: if the rule about doubts in a public area was already known from סוטה, what did יוסי בן יועזר add?
steps.deeperAnalysis: The rule was always true, but it was not taught publicly, so people were strict on themselves. יוסי בן יועזר's new step was to rule it openly. That turned a hidden leniency into a public one.

keyTerms.meaning: It is the law, but we do not rule that way publicly

phrases.english: But Rabbi Yochanan said:
It is the halacha, but we do not rule that way.
And he came and taught it as an official ruling.
phrases.notes: "He" is יוסי בן יועזר.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 17
steps.terutzResolutionType: Distinguishing what the law is from what is publicly ruled
steps.terutzHavaAmina: יוסי בן יועזר seemed to add nothing, since the rule was already known from סוטה
steps.terutzMaskana: He added an official public ruling of a rule that had not been taught openly

steps.title: A ברייתא shows the ruling was made public with stakes
steps.stepSummary: A ברייתא says that stakes were set up to mark which areas were public and which were private, so people could apply the ruling in practice.
steps.simpleTranslation: A ברייתא also teaches this: רבי יהודה says he set up stakes for them and said, up to here is a public area and up to here is a private area.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings a ברייתא that supports רבי יוחנן's explanation.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Marking the borders on the ground only makes sense if the ruling was now being put into practice publicly. Once people knew where the public area was, they could treat a doubt there as טהור.

keyTerms.meaning: A ברייתא also teaches this (a supporting source)

phrases.english: It is also taught this way:
Rabbi Yehuda says,
he drove stakes into the ground for them,
phrases.notes: "He" is יוסי בן יועזר.

phrases.english: and said: up to here is the public domain,
up to here is the private domain.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer in step 18
steps.raayaObject: The claim that יוסי בן יועזר put the leniency into public practice
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא quoting רבי יהודה about the stakes

steps.title: רבי ינאי tells people to just go immerse
steps.stepSummary: When people came to רבי ינאי with this kind of doubt, he told them to go immerse in the river.
steps.simpleTranslation: When people came before רבי ינאי, he said to them: there is deep water in the river, go immerse.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא tells a short story about how רבי ינאי handled people who had a doubt about טומאה in a public area.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Even though by the letter of the law they are טהור, רבי ינאי did not rule on the doubt. Since a river was close by, he simply sent them to immerse and end the question.

keyTerms.meaning: A deep spot, where water has collected

phrases.english: When people came before Rabbi Yannai,
phrases.notes: They came with a doubt about touching טומאה in a public area.

phrases.english: he said to them:
Here is water in a deep spot of the river,
go immerse.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: A practical story that closes the topic of the ספק טומאה ruling
steps.mimraCoreRuling: In practice, רבי ינאי told people to immerse instead of relying on the leniency
steps.whatToRemember: The rule that a ספק טומאה in a רשות הרבים is טהור was always the law. יוסי בן יועזר's contribution was ruling it publicly. Still, someone like רבי ינאי might simply tell people to immerse.

steps.title: Where do we learn that their boiled food is forbidden?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא returns to the משנה's word שלקות and asks for its source.
steps.simpleTranslation: The משנה said: and boiled foods. Where is this learned from?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא leaves the earlier topic and goes back to the משנה. It asks for the source that a נכרי's boiled food is forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The משנה listed שלקות (boiled foods of a נכרי) as forbidden. Now the גמרא wants a source for that rule, which sets up the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Boiled or cooked foods (here: cooked by a נכרי)
From where are these matters learned?

phrases.english: "And the boiled foods."
phrases.notes: These are words quoted from the משנה, which lists them among a נכרי's foods that are forbidden.

phrases.english: From where are these matters learned?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic from the משנה
steps.sheelahInformationSought: The source for forbidding a נכרי's boiled food

steps.title: Food is compared to water in משה's request
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן learns the rule from the פסוק where משה offered to pay סיחון for food and water. The food is compared to the water: unchanged, so not cooked.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי חייא בר אבא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: the פסוק says 'Sell me food for money so I may eat, and give me water for money so I may drink.' Food is like water. Just as water is unchanged, so too the food was unchanged.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers with a פסוק. Since food and water appear side by side, משה only asked to buy food that was not cooked.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Water is bought as it is, not cooked. By putting food next to water, the פסוק shows משה only wanted uncooked food. That tells us a נכרי's cooked food is forbidden.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר אַבָּא אָמַר רַבִּי יוֹחָנָן:
phrases.english: Rabbi Chiyya bar Abba said in the name of Rabbi Yochanan:
The verse says
"You shall sell me food for money, that I may eat,
phrases.notes: דברים 2:28. משה is speaking to סיחון.

phrases.english: and give me water for money, that I may drink."
Food is like water:
just as the water was not changed,
so too the food was not changed.
phrases.notes: "Not changed" here means not cooked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the שאלה of step 21
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: The comparison of food to water in משה's request shows that only unchanged (uncooked) food was bought

steps.title: Then roasted wheat should be forbidden too
steps.stepSummary: If any change makes food forbidden, a נכרי's roasted wheat would be forbidden. But a ברייתא says it is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, wheat that was made into roasted kernels should also be forbidden. And if you say yes, it is, a ברייתא teaches that wheat made into roasted kernels is permitted!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the source from step 22. It points out that the rule seems too broad.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Roasting changes the wheat, so by the rule of 'not changed' it should be forbidden. A ברייתא says it is permitted. So the comparison to water must mean something more exact.

phrases.english: But if so,
wheat that he made into roasted kernels,
would it also be forbidden?
And if you say: yes, it is,
but isn't it taught in a ברייתא:
wheat that he made into roasted kernels is permitted!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the derivation in step 22
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that any change to food makes it forbidden
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Roasted wheat is changed, yet a ברייתא permits it

steps.title: Only food changed from its natural form is forbidden
steps.stepSummary: The comparison is refined: water is unchanged from its natural form, and so the food must be unchanged from its natural form. Roasted wheat stays wheat kernels, so it is fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, food is like water: just as water is not changed from its natural state, so too the food was not changed from its natural state.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge by making the comparison to water more exact.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Being changed in some way is not enough. The food must be changed from its natural form. Roasted wheat is still recognizable kernels, so it is not changed in that way and stays permitted.

phrases.english: Rather, food is like water:
just as water was not changed from its natural state,
so too the food was not changed from its natural state.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of step 23 by refining step 22
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any change to the food forbids it
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a change from the food's natural form forbids it
steps.whatToRemember: A נכרי's cooked food is forbidden based on משה's request to סיחון: food is like water. At this point the גמרא says the forbidden change is a change from the food's natural form, which is why roasted wheat is permitted. The next step challenges this from flour, and step 26 refines it to a change made by fire.

steps.title: What about wheat ground into flour?
steps.stepSummary: If any change from natural form forbids food, then a נכרי's flour should be forbidden. But a ברייתא says flour of נכרים is permitted.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if so, wheat that a נכרי ground into flour should also be forbidden, since it is no longer in its natural form. And if you say yes, it really is forbidden, that cannot be, because a ברייתא teaches that wheat made into roasted grains, and the flours and fine flours of נכרים, are all permitted!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks the answer from the last step. Grinding wheat clearly changes it from its natural form, so by that rule flour should be forbidden.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 24 said food is forbidden only if it changed from its natural form. Flour is no longer whole kernels, so it has changed. The גמרא blocks the reply 'fine, flour is forbidden' by quoting the same ברייתא, which explicitly permits flour.

keyTerms.meaning: But now, if that is so (opens a challenge built on the last answer)
And if you say, yes, that is so

phrases.english: But now, if that is so,
wheat that he ground into flour
should it also be forbidden?
And if you say, yes, it really is,
but isn't it taught in a ברייתא:
wheat that he made into roasted grains,
phrases.notes: This is the same ברייתא from step 23. This time the גמרא focuses on its next line about flour.

phrases.english: their flours and fine flours are permitted!
phrases.notes: 'Their' means flour belonging to נכרים.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the refined comparison from step 24 (unchanged from natural form).
steps.kashyaTarget: The rule that food is forbidden only when changed from its natural form.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Grinding changes wheat's natural form, so flour should be forbidden. A ברייתא explicitly permits flour of נכרים.

steps.title: The change must be made by fire
steps.stepSummary: The comparison is narrowed again: water was not changed by fire, so the food must also not be changed by fire. Grinding is not fire, so flour is fine.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, food is like water this way: just as the water was not changed from its natural form by fire, so too the food must not be changed from its natural form by fire.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the flour challenge by adding one detail to the comparison: what matters is a change made by fire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Before, any change from natural form counted. Now only a change done through fire, meaning cooking, makes the food forbidden. Grinding is not fire, so flour stays permitted.

keyTerms.meaning: Just as ... so too (sets up a comparison)

phrases.english: Rather, food is like the water:
just as the water was not changed
from its natural form by fire,
so too the food must not be changed
from its natural form by fire.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Resolves the flour challenge of step 25 by narrowing the comparison.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrowing the comparison to one specific kind of change
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Any change from natural form, including grinding, makes the food forbidden.
steps.terutzMaskana: Only a change made by fire makes it forbidden. Grinding is not fire.

steps.title: The verse never mentions fire
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges the new answer: the פסוק says nothing about fire, so how can fire be the point of comparison?
steps.simpleTranslation: Is fire written in the פסוק at all?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא attacks step 26. The פסוק about buying food and water from סיחון never mentions fire.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The answer depended on comparing food and water through fire. But a comparison has to come from the פסוק, and fire does not appear there. So the 'fire' detail seems made up.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it at all? (a challenge meaning 'it is not')

steps.confusionAlert: This is not a real question about what the פסוק says. It means 'fire is not written,' so the answer seems unfounded.

phrases.english: Is fire written in the verse at all?
phrases.notes: He means the פסוק about סיחון from step 22, which talks about food and water but never fire.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the fire-based comparison just given in step 26.
steps.kashyaTarget: The claim that food and water are compared through not being changed by fire.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The פסוק does not mention fire, so fire cannot be the shared feature of the comparison.
